findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

background.pdr: 9-10 Hz posterior dominant rhythm, symmetric and reactive
background.sleep_features: normal vertex waves and sleep spindles

eeg.impression: Normal awake and drowsy EEG. No epileptiform discharges and no focal slowing.

alternatives: Non-hormonal options for vasomotor symptoms: lifestyle measures, cognitive behavioural therapy, SSRIs or SNRIs, gabapentin, clonidine, fezolinetant
contraindications: Migraine with aura is not a contraindication to HRT; WHO MEC and UKMEC classify contraceptives, not HRT. Combined hormonal contraception, by contrast, is UKMEC category 4 with aura.
HRT contraindications (not present in this record): current or past breast cancer, active venous or arterial thromboembolism, undiagnosed vaginal bleeding, active liver disease.
interactions: Paracetamol (current, occasional): no interaction with oestradiol or progestogens.
output.proposed: Hormone replacement therapy (oestradiol, transdermal or oral, with a progestogen)
output.summary: HRT is usable with migraine aura; transdermal oestradiol at the lowest effective dose with a progestogen carries no excess vascular risk.
warnings: Transdermal oestradiol (patch or gel) does not raise venous thromboembolism or stroke risk above baseline at standard doses, whereas oral oestrogen does; prefer transdermal at the lowest effective dose (NICE NG23).
With a uterus, add a progestogen: micronised progesterone or a levonorgestrel intrauterine system.
Fluctuating or high oestrogen doses can increase aura frequency; review if the aura changes.
HRT is not contraceptive: while still menstruating she needs contraception until menopause is confirmed; a levonorgestrel IUS provides both contraception and endometrial protection.

output.query: typical aura without headache onset or change in later life

results.finding: Typical aura not accompanied or followed within 60 minutes by headache. In some patients the headache becomes less marked or disappears with age while the aura continues; when aura without headache starts or changes in later life, the distinction from transient ischaemic attack needs careful assessment.
results.source: Headache Classification Committee of the IHS. ICHD-3. Cephalalgia 2018;38:1-211 (1.2.1.2 Typical aura without headache)

results.finding: Spreading visual and sensory symptoms that march over minutes, build up and then clear, with repeated identical episodes, distinguish late-life migraine accompaniments from ischaemic events.
results.source: Fisher CM. Late-life migraine accompaniments as a cause of unexplained transient ischemic attacks. Can J Neurol Sci 1980;7:9-17

output.summary: Aura without headache is a recognised migraine form that becomes more common with age; its march over minutes and identical repetition separate it from TIA.

output.query: hormone replacement therapy in women with migraine with aura

results.finding: Transdermal rather than oral HRT is advised for women at increased risk of venous thromboembolism; the risk of VTE with transdermal HRT at standard doses is no greater than baseline.
results.source: NICE NG23. Menopause: identification and management (2015, updated 2024)

results.finding: Migraine with aura is not a contraindication to HRT; transdermal oestrogen at the lowest dose that controls symptoms gives stable oestrogen levels and is preferred.
results.source: MacGregor EA. Migraine, menopause and hormone replacement therapy. Post Reprod Health 2018;24:11-18

output.summary: HRT is not contraindicated in migraine with aura; transdermal oestradiol at the lowest effective dose is the preferred route.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: 20 years of identical homonymous zigzag aura spreading over 20-30 minutes, now 2-3 times a month without headache: 4 of 6 C characteristics, no headache within 60 minutes; normal examination including fundi; pattern change at 48 is a red flag
action_criteria.label: Take a structured headache and aura history with examination and apply ICHD-3 criteria for typical aura without headache
action_criteria.rationale: Typical aura without headache is a clinical diagnosis; at 48 the history must show that these attacks are her long-standing aura (positive, spreading, homonymous, identical) rather than TIA or transient monocular loss.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No infarct, haemorrhage or occipital lesion; four punctate non-specific subcortical hyperintensities
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI for a change in attack pattern at 48 (aura without headache)
action_criteria.rationale: A change in attack pattern, with aura now occurring without headache in her late forties, is a red flag; MRI excludes infarction and an occipital lesion and is preferred to CT (Evans RW et al., Headache 2020;60:318-336; AAN 2000).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: HRT not contraindicated by aura; transdermal oestradiol preferred, with a progestogen for the uterus; HRT is not contraception
action_criteria.label: Check HRT before advising on her menopausal symptoms
action_criteria.rationale: She has hot flushes and asks about hormones; whether and how HRT can be used with migraine aura is the management question (NICE NG23).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on aura without headache with age and on HRT route in migraine with aura
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on aura without headache in later life and on HRT
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; the diagnosis rests on the history and examination.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not start antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for presumed TIA: the episodes have the features of migraine aura (positive visual symptoms spreading over 20-30 minutes, identical to 20 years of previous auras) and imaging shows no infarct.
Do not continue or start combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring): migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4; offer a progestogen-only method or an IUD.
required_recommendations: Explain that the episodes are her usual visual aura without the headache (ICHD-3 1.2.1.2), a recognised change with age and around the menopause, and that her history, examination and MRI show no sign of TIA or structural disease.

If HRT is wanted for menopausal symptoms, migraine with aura is not a contraindication: prefer transdermal oestradiol at the lowest effective dose, with micronised progesterone or a levonorgestrel IUS for endometrial protection, and review if the aura changes (NICE NG23).
Discuss contraception until the menopause is confirmed: combined methods are UKMEC category 4 with aura, and a levonorgestrel IUS gives contraception and, with oestradiol, endometrial protection.

No acute or preventive migraine medicine is needed for brief non-disabling aura without headache; ask her to keep a diary and to seek review if an aura lasts over 60 minutes, changes character or brings new symptoms.

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis; neither is present here

Routine transthoracic or bubble echocardiography (PFO screening) is not indicated in migraine with aura without stroke; PFO closure does not treat migraine (PREMIUM, Tobis JM et al., JACC 2017; PRIMA, Mattle HP et al., Eur Heart J 2016; MIST, Dowson A et al., Circulation 2008).
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; no role unless cardioembolic stroke is on the differential
EEG is not indicated for migraine with aura; reserve for cases where focal seizure is genuinely on the differential

accepted: Typical aura without headache (ICHD-3 1.2.1.2, acephalgic migraine) — emerging perimenopausal phenotype change in established migraine with aura

differential.key_features: Positive zigzag lights expanding over 20-30 minutes, identical to 20 years of aura and recurring 2-3 times a month, in a normotensive non-smoker; TIA symptoms are usually negative and maximal at onset. MRI shows no infarct.
Amaurosis is monocular, negative and abrupt; her symptom is homonymous (persists with either eye closed) and positive; fundi and retinal vessels normal.
Occipital seizures give brief coloured circular phenomena lasting seconds to a few minutes; her zigzag crescent spreads over 20-30 minutes; MRI shows normal occipital lobes.
Under 50, no new headache, jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, systemic symptoms or monocular loss.

key_clinical_evidence: 20 years of migraine with typical visual aura; for 12-18 months the same homonymous zigzag aura, spreading over 20-30 minutes, occurs 2-3 times a month without headache: typical aura without headache (ICHD-3 1.2.1.2).
The pattern change at 48 justifies MRI, which shows no infarct or occipital lesion; four punctate non-specific white matter hyperintensities are common in migraine.
Migraine with aura is not a contraindication to HRT: transdermal oestradiol at the lowest effective dose with a progestogen is preferred; combined hormonal contraception remains UKMEC category 4.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The aura is identical to 20 years of her typical aura: positive, homonymous and spreading over 20-30 minutes; only the headache has gone.
red_herrings.data_point: Visual episodes without headache in a 48-year-old who has read that they could be TIA or retinal artery occlusion
red_herrings.intended_effect: May anchor on TIA or amaurosis and lead to antiplatelet therapy or a vascular work-up

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: HRT is not contraindicated by aura: transdermal oestradiol at the lowest effective dose with a progestogen is preferred (NICE NG23).
red_herrings.data_point: Hot flushes and irregular periods; combined pill stopped 18 years ago because of migraine
red_herrings.intended_effect: May lead to the conclusion that HRT is contraindicated, as the combined pill is

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Small non-specific subcortical hyperintensities are common in migraine with aura; there is no infarct.
red_herrings.data_point: Four punctate subcortical white matter hyperintensities on MRI
red_herrings.intended_effect: May be read as small-vessel ischaemia supporting TIA

sequence_constraints.reason: The structured history identifies the red flag (change in attack pattern) that justifies imaging.

findings.result: 20 years of attacks of visual aura followed by right-sided throbbing headache. For 12-18 months, 2-3 attacks a month of the same aura without headache, or with a brief mild headache (1-2/10).
Visual only: an expanding crescent of shimmering zigzag lights on one side of vision, still present with either eye closed. No sensory, speech, motor or brainstem symptom. Fully reversible.
The crescent expands gradually over 20-30 minutes.
Unilateral (one visual hemifield), the same pattern as in the past 20 years.
Absent in most recent attacks; previously a right-sided throbbing headache followed every aura.

Visual fields full to confrontation, discs and retinal vessels normal, eye movements normal, power 5/5 without drift, sensation intact, reflexes 2+ and symmetric, plantars flexor, coordination and gait normal. BP 124/78 mmHg.

Change in attack pattern (loss of headache after 20 years) at 48: present. Systemic symptoms, history of neoplasm, persisting deficit, thunderclap onset, age over 50 at onset, positional or Valsalva trigger, papilloedema, progressive headache, pregnancy, painful eye, head trauma, immune suppression and analgesic overuse: absent. No jaw claudication, scalp tenderness or transient monocular loss.
Perimenopausal: cycles every 6-8 weeks, hot flushes. No HRT; combined pill stopped 18 years ago. Paracetamol occasionally. Non-smoker; no hypertension or diabetes.

clinical_assessment.impression:
1. Long-standing migraine with typical aura; the current attacks are the same visual aura without headache: ICHD-3 1.2 met (4 of 6 C characteristics) with no headache within 60 minutes. Supports typical aura without headache (ICHD-3 1.2.1.2).
2. Homonymous, positive, gradually spreading visual symptoms identical to her previous auras; no features of transient monocular visual loss.
3. Red flag present: change in attack pattern at 48.

scores.ICHD-3 criterion C characteristics met: 4 of 6 (at least 3 required): spread, duration, unilateral, positive; succession absent, headache now absent

additional_observations: No restricted diffusion on DWI and ADC.
Occipital lobes and visual pathways normal; no occipital mass or cortical malformation.
No haemorrhage or microhaemorrhage on susceptibility-weighted imaging; no abnormal flow voids.
Ventricles, sulci and posterior fossa normal for age.

findings.location: Bilateral frontal and parietal subcortical white matter (four foci)

mri.impression:
1. No infarct, haemorrhage or occipital lesion.
2. Four punctate frontal and parietal subcortical white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensities, non-specific.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 48-year-old British woman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic concerned about episodes of visual disturbance without headache that have been occurring approximately twice monthly for the past year. She has a 20-year history of migraine with visual aura and headache — typical expanding crescent of shimmering zigzag lights over 20-30 minutes followed by a right-sided throbbing headache. Over the past 12-18 months, her episodes have gradually changed: she still gets the identical visual aura, but the headache that used to follow is now absent or minimal (1-2/10) and brief. She has 2-3 'visual-only' episodes per month.

She is worried about these episodes because she read that visual disturbances in her age group without headache could be TIA or retinal artery occlusion. She is also perimenopausal — periods are now irregular (every 6-8 weeks) — and has noticed hot flushes. She wonders if the hormonal changes are connected. She has no prior TIA or stroke. She is a non-smoker, normal blood pressure, and recently had a health check which she says was 'all normal.' She is not on any hormone replacement therapy. She had her combined OCP stopped 18 years ago after her migraines were diagnosed. She currently uses paracetamol occasionally when a mild headache follows the aura. Her two adult daughters both have migraines.
